p.src: The story tells how the Tang Monk, having regained Sun Wukong, journeyed westward with his disciples, all united in heart and purpose. After rescuing the princess of the Kingdom of Baoxiang, they were escorted westward out of the city by the sovereign and his ministers. There is no telling all the times they ate when hungry and drank when thirsty, lodged by night and travelled at dawn. Once again they came upon the season of spring, and at that time:

p.src: As master and disciples travelled on admiring the scenery, they saw another mountain blocking their way. The Tang Monk said, “Disciples, be careful. A lofty mountain lies ahead, and I fear tigers and wolves may bar our way.” Wukong said, “Master, a man who has left the household should not speak as though he still lived within it. Do you remember the words in the Heart Sutra taught by the Monk of the Crow’s Nest: ‘With no hindrance in the mind—and because there is no hindrance—there is no fear, and one is far removed from inverted dreams and delusions’? You need only ‘sweep the grime from your heart and wash the dust from beside your ears. Unless one endures the bitterest of hardships, one can hardly become the foremost among men.’ Do not give way to anxiety. So long as old Sun is here, even if the sky should fall, I can keep you safe. Why fear any tiger or wolf?” The elder reined back his horse and said, “I—”

The elder reined back his horse and said, “I—”

p.src: Hearing this, Wukong chuckled and said, “If Master wishes to be free of worldly cares, what difficulty is there in that? Once our undertaking is accomplished, all entanglements will cease and all phenomena will be empty. When that time comes, it will happen of itself. Will you not then be free of worldly cares?” On hearing these words, the elder could only take comfort and forget his worries. He loosened the reins and urged on his silver-hoofed, jade-dragon steed.

p.src: He shouted sternly to the elder, “You elder travelling westward, halt for a moment! I have a word of warning for you: a band of vicious demons and savage monsters dwells on this mountain, and they make a special prey of travellers going east or west.” At these words, the elder’s soul fled and his wits deserted him. Trembling so violently that he could scarcely stay in the carved saddle, he hurriedly turned and called to his disciples, “Did you hear the woodcutter’s warning? ‘There are vicious demons and savage monsters on this mountain.’ Who dares go and question him closely?” Wukong said, “Set your mind at ease, Master. Let old Sun go and learn the truth from him.”

u.src: He shouted sternly to the elder, “You elder travelling westward, halt for a moment! I have a word of warning for you: a band of vicious demons and savage monsters dwells on this mountain, and they make a special prey of travellers going east or west.”

At these words, the elder’s soul fled and his wits deserted him. Trembling so violently that he could scarcely stay in the carved saddle, he hurriedly turned and called to his disciples, “Did you hear the woodcutter’s warning? ‘There are vicious demons and savage monsters on this mountain.’
Who dares go and question him closely?”
Wukong said, “Set your mind at ease, Master. Let old Sun go and learn the truth from him.”

p.src: Good Wukong strode swiftly straight up the mountain, called the woodcutter “Brother,” and saluted him. Returning the salute, the woodcutter said, “Elder, what brings you people here?” Wukong said, “To tell you the truth, Brother, we were sent from the Land of the East to fetch scriptures from the Western Heaven. The one on horseback is my master, and he is somewhat timid. You were kind enough just now to warn us of some vicious demon or savage monster, so I have come to ask: how long has this demon been a demon, and how long has this monster been a monster? Is he an old hand, or merely a novice? Please tell me honestly, Brother, so that I can have the mountain god and the local earth god escort him away under guard.” Hearing this, the woodcutter threw back his head and laughed. “So you are a mad monk after all.” Wukong said, “I am not mad. I speak the honest truth.” The woodcutter said, “If you are speaking honestly, how dare you say you will have him escorted away?” Wukong said, “You praise his might like this and talk nonsense to stop us with a warning—are you perhaps related to him? If not kin, you must be a neighbour; if not a neighbour, then surely a friend.” The woodcutter laughed. “You mad, impudent monk, you are utterly unreasonable. I came especially out of goodwill to warn you, so that you would keep watch day and night as you travelled, yet you turn around and lay the blame on me. Never mind that I do not know where those demons came from—even if I did, how would you dare have them escorted away? Where would you escort them to?” Wukong said, “If it is a heavenly demon, I will send it to the Jade Emperor; if it is an earthly demon, I will send it to the earthly authorities. Those of the West go to the Buddha, and those of the East go to the sages; those of the North are sent to Zhenwu, and those of the South to the God of Fire. A dragon-fiend is sent to the Lord of the Seas, and an evil ghost to the King of Hell. Each has its own proper jurisdiction and destination. Old Sun has acquaintances everywhere. I will issue a writ and have him rushed away under guard that very night.”

p.src: The woodcutter could not suppress a scornful chuckle. “You mad, impudent monk, I suppose you have wandered about the countryside and learned a few arts of drawing talismans and blessing water. Such tricks may drive off evil spirits and bind ghosts, but you have never yet encountered monsters as vicious as these.” Wukong said, “What makes you say they are so vicious?” The woodcutter said, “The path through this mountain runs for roughly six hundred li, and the place is called Flat-Top Mountain. Within the mountain is a cave called Lotus Cave. Two demon chiefs live in that cave. They have drawn likenesses and issued descriptions in order to capture monks; they have copied down names and made inquiries because they mean to eat the Tang Monk. If you had come from anywhere else, you might be all right; but if the word ‘Tang’ applies to you, do not dream that you can escape—escape.” Wukong said, “We have indeed come from the Tang dynasty.” The woodcutter said, “Then it is precisely you they want to eat.” Wukong said, “What splendid luck, splendid luck! But I wonder how they eat their victims?” The woodcutter said, “How would you like them to eat you?” Wukong said, “If they eat the head first, that would be quite amusing; but if they eat the feet first, that would be hard to bear.” The woodcutter said, “What do you mean by eating the head first? And what do you mean by eating the feet first?” Wukong said, “You have never experienced it yourself. If they eat the head first, they will bite it off in one mouthful and I shall already be dead. Then however they fry, sauté, stew, or boil me, I shall feel no pain. But if they eat the feet first, gnawing my ankles, chewing my shins, and eating their way up to my waist, I shall be in agony without dying quickly. Would that not mean suffering bit by bit? That is why it would be hard to bear.” The woodcutter said, “Monk, they have no time for all that. They simply seize you, tie you inside a steamer, and steam you whole before eating you.” Wukong laughed. “That is even better, even better. It will not be unbearably painful; I shall merely have to endure a little stifling steam.” The woodcutter said, “Monk, stop your flippant talk. Those monsters carry five treasures with them, and their magical powers are immense and far-reaching. Even if you were the jade pillar that props up heaven or the golden beam that spans the sea, to protect the monk from the Tang dynasty on his way through, you would still have to suffer a few fainting fits.” Wukong said, “How many fainting fits?” The woodcutter said, “Three or four.” Wukong said, “That is nothing, nothing at all. In a year we commonly suffer seven or eight hundred fainting fits. Three or four are easy enough—we shall faint a few times and soon be over them.”

p.src: The Great Sage, as admirable as ever, was utterly unafraid; his sole concern was to protect the Tang Monk. He broke away from the woodcutter, strode back, and went straight to the horse at the foot of the slope. “Master,” he said, “it is nothing serious. There are indeed a few minor fiends here, but the local people are timid and take them too seriously. With me here, what is there to fear from them? Let us go, let us go.” Hearing this, the elder could only set aside his fears and follow on. As they continued on, they soon found that the woodcutter had vanished. The elder said, “How did that woodcutter who warned us disappear so quickly?” Bajie said, “Our luck must be poor—we have run into a ghost in broad daylight.” Wukong said, “I expect he went into the woods to gather firewood. Let me go and have a look.”

p.src: The Great Sage opened his Fiery Eyes and Golden Pupils and searched across the mountains and beyond the ridges, but saw no trace of anyone. Suddenly he looked up into the clouds and saw that it was the Duty Officer of the Day. He sprang onto a cloud and caught up with him, cursed him several times as a “hairy wretch,” and said, “Why did you not come and tell me plainly what you had to say? Why did you transform yourself like that and put on an act for Old Sun?” The officer hastily bowed and said, “Great Sage, forgive me, forgive me for bringing the warning so late. That monster truly possesses vast powers and countless transformations. You must summon all your cleverness, exercise your divine ingenuity, and guard your master with the greatest care; if you grow careless in the slightest, you may forget all hope of reaching the Western Heaven.”

p.src: Hearing this, the pilgrim dismissed the officer with a rebuke, engraved the warning deeply in his heart, lowered his cloud, and returned straight to the mountain. There he saw the elder proceeding with Bajie and Sha Monk clustered around him. He thought to himself, “If I tell Master exactly what the officer said, he is so feeble that he will surely start crying; but if I do not tell him the truth and simply lead him blindly onward, as the saying goes, ‘When first entering a reed marsh, one knows not how deep it is.’ If a demon should snatch him away, would Old Sun not have to trouble himself all over again? Let me put Bajie to the test first and send him out to fight the monster. If he can defeat it, the achievement shall count as his; if he lacks the skill and is captured, Old Sun can still go and rescue him afterward, and that will nicely display my own prowess and spread my fame.” While pondering this, he questioned himself inwardly: “I only fear that Bajie will shirk the work and refuse to take the lead, while Master is rather inclined to shield his shortcomings. Let Old Sun put some pressure on him.”

p.src: Now look at the Great Sage: he put on a false show, rubbed his eyes, and squeezed out a few tears. He met his master and walked straight ahead. When Bajie saw him, he hurriedly cried, “Brother Sha, put down the carrying pole and take out the luggage. Let the two of us divide it.” Sha Monk said, “Second Elder Brother, why should we divide it?” Bajie said, “Let us divide it and be done. You can return to the River of Flowing Sands and become a monster again, while Old Pig will go back to Gao Village to see his wife. We shall sell the white horse, buy a coffin, and see Master properly to his grave. Then everyone can break up. What is the use of still going to the Western Heaven?” Hearing this from his horse, the elder said, “You oaf! We are properly on our journey, so why are you talking nonsense again?” Bajie said, “It is your precious son who is talking nonsense. Can you not see Sun the Pilgrim coming over there in tears? He is a hero who can bore into heaven or burrow into earth and fears neither axes, fire, nor even being dropped into a cauldron of boiling oil; yet now he comes with a cap of sorrow on his head and tears in his eyes. The mountain must be perilous and the monsters ferocious. How could weaklings like us possibly get through?” The elder said, “Stop talking nonsense for now. Let me ask him and hear what he has to say.” He asked, “Wukong, if there is something to discuss, say it to my face. Why are you grieving by yourself? Why have you put on such a tearful face? Are you trying to frighten me?” The pilgrim said, “Master, the one who brought the warning just now was the Duty Officer of the Day. He said the fiend was ferocious and this place hard to cross. Indeed, the mountain is high and the path steep, and we cannot advance. Let us go another day.” At these words the elder was terrified. Grasping the pilgrim by his tiger-skin kilt, he said, “Disciple, of the three parts of our journey we have already covered more than half. Why do you now speak of turning back?” The pilgrim said, “It is not that I would fail to do my utmost. I merely fear there are many demons while our strength is slight, and I must face them alone. ‘Even if one has a block of iron, how many nails can it yield once put to the forge?’” The elder said, “Disciple, what you say is true. It is indeed hard for one man alone. The military books say, ‘The few cannot withstand the many.’ But here are Bajie and Sha Monk, who are disciples too. Command and employ them as you see fit, whether as guards or helpers. If you join your strength and purpose, clear the mountain path, and lead me across, will you not all attain the true fruit together?”

p.src: All the pilgrim's affected hesitation had been intended only to coax these words from the elder. Wiping away his tears, he said, “Master, if we are to cross this mountain, Zhu Bajie must agree to two conditions of mine. Only then shall we have even a three-in-ten chance of passing; if he will not obey me and lend me a hand, we have not the slightest hope of getting through.” Bajie said, “Elder Brother, if we cannot go on, let us simply break up. Do not drag me into it.” The elder said, “Disciple, first ask your elder brother what he wants you to do.” The idiot then actually said to the pilgrim, “Brother, what do you want me to do?” The pilgrim said, “The first task is to look after Master; the second is to patrol the mountain.” Bajie said, “Looking after Master means sitting still, while patrolling the mountain means walking about. Surely you do not expect me to sit awhile and then walk, and walk awhile and then sit? How could I attend to both places?” The pilgrim said, “I am not telling you to do both together. You need only take one of them.” Bajie laughed again and said, “In that case, it is worth discussing. But what exactly does looking after Master involve, and what does patrolling the mountain involve? Explain them to me first, and I shall choose the one that suits me better.” The pilgrim said, “If you look after Master, then when he goes to relieve himself, you must wait upon him; when Master wishes to travel, you must support him; and when Master wants a vegetarian meal, you must beg one for him. If he goes even a little hungry, you deserve a beating; if his face grows even a little sallow, you deserve a beating; and if his body grows even a little thin, you deserve a beating.” Bajie panicked and said, “That is hard, hard, hard! Waiting upon him and supporting him are no great trouble; even carrying him constantly on my back would still be easy; but if I am sent into a village to beg for food, the people on this western road will not recognize me as a scripture-seeking monk. They will only think I am some half-grown, burly pig that has wandered out of the mountains. A whole crowd will gather with forks, rakes, and brooms, surround Old Pig, knock him down, take him home, slaughter him, and salt him for the New Year. Would that not be a cursed fate?” The pilgrim said, “Then go patrol the mountain.” Bajie said, “And what does patrolling the mountain involve?” The pilgrim said, “Enter this mountain and find out how many monsters there are, what the mountain is called, and what cave they live in, so that we may get through.” Bajie said, “That is a trifling matter. Old Pig will go patrol the mountain.” The idiot hitched up his robe, held his nine-pronged rake upright, and marched valiantly straight into the deep mountains; with head held high and spirits soaring, he strode onto the main road.

Bajie said, “And what does patrolling the mountain involve?”
The pilgrim said, “Enter this mountain and find out how many monsters there are, what the mountain is called, and what cave they live in, so that we may get through.”
Bajie said, “That is a trifling matter. Old Pig will go patrol the mountain.”
The idiot hitched up his robe, held his nine-pronged rake upright, and marched valiantly straight into the deep mountains;
with head held high and spirits soaring, he strode onto the main road.

p.src: The Pilgrim, standing nearby, could not help giving a scornful chuckle. The elder scolded him: “You impudent monkey! You show your brothers no affection at all and are forever harboring jealousy toward them. You played this sly trick, putting on a winning face and coaxing him into going on some mountain patrol, and now you stand here laughing at him.” The Pilgrim said, “I am not laughing at him. There is meaning in my laughter. Just watch: Zhu Bajie will certainly not patrol the mountain, nor will he dare face any monster. He will hide somewhere for a while, concoct a lie, and come back to fool us.” The elder asked, “How can you know what he will do?” The Pilgrim replied, “I judge that this is exactly what he will do. If you do not believe me, let me follow him, watch what he does, and hear what he says. For one thing, I can lend him a hand in subduing monsters; for another, I can see whether he is truly sincere in worshiping the Buddha.” The elder said, “Very well, very well. But do not go tormenting him.” The Pilgrim agreed and hurried straight up the slope. With a shake of his body, he transformed himself into a tiny cicada-like insect. It was indeed a light and nimble transformation. Just look at him:

p.src: With a chirp and a flap of his wings, he flew after Bajie and clung beneath the roots of the bristles behind his ear. The fool simply trudged on, never suspecting that someone was riding on him. After traveling seven or eight li, he threw down his rake, turned back toward Tang Sanzang, and cursed with wild gestures: “You feeble old monk! You spiteful Bimawen! You meek-faced Friar Sand! All of you stay there at ease while you send old Zhu trudging over these roads. We are all going to fetch the scriptures and all hope to attain the true fruit, so why must I alone be sent to patrol some mountain? Ha! When you know there are monsters, it is still not enough to give them a wide berth; they insist on sending me to seek them out. What rotten luck! I shall find somewhere to sleep. After a good nap, I will go back and give them some vague answer, say I patrolled the mountain, and that will settle the account.” Congratulating himself on his clever escape, the fool hoisted his rake and walked on until he saw a curved slope covered in red grass within a hollow. He plunged straight into it, raked together a bed on the ground, rolled down upon it, stretched his back, and exclaimed, “What bliss! Not even that Bimawen can be as carefree as I am.”

p.src: This bird was neither large nor small; weighed on a scale, it would be only two or three ounces. It had a red-copper beak and black-iron feet. With a whir of its wings, it swooped down. Bajie lay fast asleep on his back when the bird struck him sharply on the lip.

p.src: The fool scrambled up in terror, shouting wildly, “A monster! A monster! It stabbed me with a spear and fled! Oh, how my mouth hurts!” He felt it with his hand and brought away a smear of blood. He said, “What wretched luck! Nothing fortunate has happened to me, so why am I wearing red upon my lips?” Staring at his bloodied hand, he muttered endlessly and looked all around, but saw no sign of anything. He said, “If there is no monster, what stabbed me with a spear?” Suddenly he raised his head and looked upward. There was a woodpecker flying in midair. Grinding his teeth, the fool cursed, “You wretched creature! It is bad enough that Bimawen bullies me; now you come to bully me too. I understand now. It must not recognize me as a man. It took my snout for a length of black, rotten, decaying wood with grubs inside, and pecked me while hunting for something to eat. I shall tuck my snout inside my robe and sleep.” The fool rolled over and lay down to sleep again. The Pilgrim flew back and pecked him once more behind the ear. The fool scrambled up in alarm and said, “You wretched bird, you are truly giving me no peace! This must be where its nest is. It has laid eggs and is raising chicks, and fears I have taken its place; that is why it keeps troubling me. Enough, enough! I will not sleep here anymore.” He hoisted his rake, went straight out of the red-grass slope, found the path, and walked on. Sun Wukong was delighted beyond measure; the Handsome Monkey King nearly collapsed with laughter. The Pilgrim said, “That oaf has two great eyes wide open, yet he cannot even recognize one of his own companions.”

p.src: The Great Sage gave his body another shake, changed back into the tiny cicada-like insect, and clung behind Bajie’s ear, never leaving him. The fool went deeper into the mountain and traveled another four or five li. In a hollow he saw three square slabs of blue stone, each as broad as a tabletop. The fool set down his rake and made a deep ceremonial bow to the stones. The Pilgrim laughed inwardly: “What a fool! Stones are not people; they cannot speak or return his courtesy. Why bow to them? Is he not utterly witless?” In fact, the fool was treating the three stones as Tang Sanzang, Friar Sand, and the Pilgrim, and was rehearsing before them. He said, “When I return and see Master, if he asks whether there are monsters, I shall say there are monsters. If he asks what sort of mountain it is, I cannot say it was kneaded from mud, made from earth, hammered from tin, cast from copper, steamed from dough, pasted from paper, or drawn with a brush. They already call me a fool, and if I say such things, they will think me more foolish still. I shall simply say it was a stone mountain. If he asks what sort of cave, I shall simply say it was a stone cave. If he asks what sort of gate, I shall say it was an iron-plated gate studded with nails. If he asks how far it went inside, I shall say there were three levels within. If he presses his questions further and asks how many nails were in the gate, I shall say old Zhu was in such a hurry that he cannot remember clearly. Now that I have made the whole story up, I can go and fool that Bimawen.” Having pieced together his fabrication, the fool dragged his rake and headed straight back along the road by which he had come.

p.src: Little did he know that the Pilgrim, hidden behind his ear, had heard every word clearly. When the Pilgrim saw him turning back, he spread his wings, flew ahead, resumed his true form, and went to see his master. His master asked, “Wukong, you are back. Why has Wuneng not returned?” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “He is over there concocting lies. He will be here presently.” The elder said, “His two ears almost cover his eyes, and he is a simple fool. What lie could he possibly concoct? You must be making up some devilish tale to lay the blame on him again.” The Pilgrim said, “Master, you are always shielding his faults like this. This time there will be questions by which his story can be tested.” He then told them in advance how Bajie had burrowed into the grass to sleep, been awakened by a woodpecker’s peck, bowed to the stones, and fabricated a tale about a stone mountain, a stone cave, an iron-plated gate, and monsters.

p.src: When he had finished speaking, before long the fool came walking back. Afraid he might forget his lie, he kept his head lowered and rehearsed it under his breath. The Pilgrim shouted at him, “Fool, what are you muttering?” Bajie pricked up his ears, looked around, and said, “Have I arrived already?” The fool went forward and fell to his knees. The elder helped him up and said, “Disciple, you have had a hard journey.” Bajie said, “Indeed. Of all people, travelers and mountain climbers have it hardest.” The elder asked, “Were there any monsters?” Bajie said, “There were monsters—monsters everywhere, a whole horde of them!” The elder asked, “Then how did they let you return?” Bajie said, “They called me Grandfather Pig and Great-Grandfather Pig, prepared some vermicelli soup and vegetarian food, and fed me a meal. They said they would parade their banners and drums and escort us across the mountain.” The Pilgrim said, “I expect you fell asleep in the grass and are recounting a dream.” At these words the fool shrank two inches in fright and thought, “Good heavens! How did he know I was asleep?” The Pilgrim stepped forward, seized him, and said, “Come here and answer my questions.” The fool panicked again and said, trembling, “Ask if you wish; why grab and tug at me?” The Pilgrim asked, “What mountain was it?” Bajie answered, “Stone Mountain.” “What cave?” He answered, “Stone Cave.” “What sort of gate?” He answered, “An iron-plated gate studded with nails.” “How far does it go inside?” He answered, “There are three levels within.” The Pilgrim said, “You need say no more. I remember the latter half perfectly. Since Master may not believe you, I shall finish it for you.” Bajie said, “You ugly mug! You never went there. What could you know that you would speak for me?” The Pilgrim laughed. “‘As for how many nails were on the gate, just say that Old Pig was flustered and could not remember clearly.’ Is that not right?” The fool immediately fell to his knees in alarm. The Pilgrim said, “You bowed to a rock, pretended it was the three of us, and questioned and answered yourself. Is that not so? Then you said, ‘Let me get my lie straight and go fool that Stable-Keeper.’ Is that not right?” The fool merely kowtowed again and again, saying, “Elder Brother, when I went to patrol the mountain, could you possibly have followed and listened?”

p.src: The Pilgrim cursed him: “You useless, bran-stuffed oaf! At such a perilous place, I sent you to patrol the mountain, yet you went to sleep. Had the woodpecker not pecked you awake, you would still be sleeping there. And once awakened, you concocted such an enormous lie. Might that not have ruined our great undertaking? Quickly stick out your shin, and I shall give you five strokes to teach you a lesson.” Bajie panicked. “That mourning staff is heavy: a mere graze will split my skin, and a slight swing will tear my sinews; five blows would kill me.” The Pilgrim said, “If you fear a beating, why did you lie?” Bajie said, “Elder Brother, it was only this once. I shall never dare do it again.” The Pilgrim said, “For one offense, three strokes.” Bajie cried, “Mercy! I could not endure even half a stroke.” At his wits’ end, the fool clutched his master and said, “Please put in a good word for me.” The elder said, “When Wukong said you had invented a lie, I did not believe him; now that it proves true, you indeed deserve a beating. But while crossing this mountain we have few hands to command. Wukong, spare him for now, until we have crossed it. Beat him afterward.” The Pilgrim said, “The ancients said, ‘To comply with one’s parents’ wishes and feelings is called great filial piety.’ Since Master says not to beat you, I shall spare you for the moment. Go patrol the mountain for him once more. If you lie again and endanger our undertaking, I shall certainly not spare you a single blow.”

p.src: The fool had no choice but to get up and go again. Once he reached the main road, his guilty conscience bred phantoms: at every step he suspected that the Pilgrim had transformed himself and was following him, so whatever he saw he took for the Pilgrim. After going seven or eight li, he saw a tiger run across the mountainside. Unafraid, he raised his rake and said, “Elder Brother, have you come to listen for lies? I shall make up nothing this time.” He went on. A fierce mountain wind came roaring through, blew down a dead tree, and rolled it before him. Stamping his feet and beating his chest, he cried, “Brother, what is the meaning of this? I have already said I dare not invent lies. Why turn into a tree to strike me?” Going farther, he saw a white-necked crow overhead caw several times in succession. He said again, “Elder Brother, shame on you, shame on you! I said I would not invent anything, and I will not. Why persist in turning into a crow? Have you come to listen?” In fact, this time the Pilgrim had not followed him at all. The fool was frightening himself, imagining and suspecting things at random, and wherever he went he thought the Pilgrim was following at his side. We shall say no more for now of the fool’s alarms and suspicions.

p.src: Now the mountain was called Flat-Top Mountain, and the cave was called Lotus Cave. Two monsters lived in the cave: one was called Great King Gold Horn, the other Great King Silver Horn. Gold Horn was sitting there when he said to Silver Horn, “Brother, how long has it been since we patrolled the mountain?” Silver Horn replied, “Half a month.” Gold Horn said, “Brother, go make a patrol for me today.” Silver Horn asked, “Why patrol the mountain today?” Gold Horn said, “You do not know. I recently heard that the Tang court in the Eastern Land sent the imperial brother, the Tang Monk, westward to worship the Buddha. His party numbers four—the ones called Sun the Pilgrim, Zhu Bajie, and Friar Sand—and with the horse they are five mouths in all. Find where they are and capture them for me.” Silver Horn said, “If we want to eat people, we can catch any number anywhere. When this monk gets here, let him pass.” Gold Horn said, “You do not understand. When I left the celestial realm years ago, I heard it said that the Tang Monk is the Elder Golden Cicada incarnated in the mortal world, a good man cultivated through ten lifetimes whose primal yang has never leaked away. Whoever eats his flesh will enjoy long life and immortality.” Silver Horn said, “If eating his flesh grants long life and immortality, why should we meditate, perform meritorious works, refine the dragon and tiger, or pair female and male? We should simply eat him. Let me go capture him.” Gold Horn said, “Brother, you are somewhat hasty. Do not rush. If you go out and, without regard for right or wrong, seize every monk you see, it would be most improper if he were not the Tang Monk. I remember their appearances and once had likenesses drawn of the master and his disciples. Take the picture with you, and whenever you meet a monk, compare him against it carefully.” He then explained, one by one, which person bore which name. Once Silver Horn had received the portraits and learned the names, he left the cave, mustered thirty lesser monsters, and came up the mountain on patrol.

p.src: Now, as ill luck would have it, Bajie was on his way when he ran straight into the band of demons, who blocked his path and demanded, “Who are you, and where have you come from?” The fool raised his head and pricked up his ears. When he saw that they were demons, he panicked and thought to himself, “If I say I’m a scripture-seeking monk, they’ll seize me at once.” So he merely said that he was a traveler passing through. A lesser demon reported back, “Great King, he says he’s a traveler.” Among the thirty lesser demons, some recognized him and some did not. One standing nearby, who had heard the descriptions given earlier, said, “Great King, this monk looks like Zhu Bajie in the picture.” They ordered the portrait to be hung up. When Bajie saw it, he was greatly alarmed and said, “No wonder I’ve felt so listless lately—they’ve brought my very likeness here!” A lesser demon held the picture aloft on the tip of his spear, while Silver Horn pointed at it and said, “The one riding the white horse is the Tang Monk, and the hairy-faced one is Sun the Novice. …” Hearing this, Bajie murmured, “God of the City, if I’m not in it, all shall be well; I’ll offer you a whole pig’s head and twenty-four portions of offerings for a grand purification rite.” He kept muttering under his breath, making promise after promise. The demon went on, “This tall black fellow is Monk Sha, and this one with the long snout and great ears is Zhu Bajie.” When the fool heard himself mentioned, he was so frightened that he tucked his snout into his robe to hide it. p.src: When the demon heard this, he had no intention of yielding. Wielding his Seven-Star Sword and bringing all his techniques into play, he traded blow for blow with Bajie. They fought twenty rounds in the mountains without either gaining the upper hand. Bajie grew fierce and met him with utter disregard for his own life. The demon saw him twitching his ears, spraying sticky spittle, whirling his rake, and bellowing at the top of his voice. Feeling somewhat alarmed himself, he turned and called to the lesser demons to attack together. Had it remained one against one, Bajie would in truth have fared well enough. But when he saw all the lesser demons swarm upon him, he lost his composure. Unable to parry them all, he was beaten and turned to flee. The path was rough, and as he had not watched his footing carefully, he was suddenly caught by a trailing vine and stumbled. He struggled up and had just started running again when a lesser demon, lying flat on the ground, grabbed his heel and sent him sprawling face-first once more. The whole mob overtook and pinned him down. Some grabbed his bristles, some yanked his ears, some pulled his legs, and others tugged his tail; then, heaving and hauling, they carried him captive into the cave. Ah! Just as the saying goes:
